title: Crimes and Online Safety Legislation Amendment (Combatting Online Notoriety) Bill 2024
short_title: Crimes and Online Safety Legislation Amendment (Combatting Online Notoriety) Bill 2024

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would create a Commonwealth offence of posting harmful material online to increase notoriety and extend the eSafety Commissioner's powers to criminal activity material.
A person who posts material showing violence or apparent drug or property offences, intending to raise their own notoriety or that of people depicted, would face up to two years' imprisonment.

Journalism, genuine scientific, academic, educational, artistic, literary or satirical purposes, reasonable excuse and protected political communication would be defences, and merely filming or re-posting such material would not be caught.
changes: Intention would be the fault element for the posting and the notoriety purpose, and recklessness for whether the material shows violence or apparent drug or property offences.
The Online Safety Act 2021 would define criminal activity material as material on such services that constitutes or may constitute a criminal offence and was posted to gain notoriety.

The eSafety Commissioner would run a complaints system for criminal activity material, investigate complaints and be able to issue removal notices to service providers, hosting providers or the poster.
Failing to comply with a removal notice could attract a civil penalty of $156,500 or 500 penalty units, with Commissioner decisions reviewable by the Administrative Appeals Tribunal.
The Crimes Act 1914 would let a court order a person convicted of the new offence to stop using, or only conditionally use, specified online services for up to two years.
summary.affected: People who post material online, social media, electronic and internet service providers, hosting providers, the eSafety Commissioner, courts and journalists are affected.
